description:
SYNTRA is a multidisciplinary tech team from Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, combining expertise in AI/ML, Data Engineering, Cloud Computing, Software Development, and Data Analytics. We transform complex data into intelligent, scalable solutions through innovation, precision, and engineering excellence. Tackling NASA's MODIS & VIIRS challenge, we aim to turn satellite data into actionable insights for smarter wildfire monitoring.

We don't just analyze data. We engineer impact.
summary:
SYNTRA is a website and app that turn 26 years of NASA fire detections over Sudan into one consistent fire record, plus an early warning that updates every 30 minutes.

What we developed: a pipeline that cleans NASA FIRMS hotspots and counts them on a 0.1° grid. It then converts MODIS into VIIRS units with month-by-month factors fitted on the years both sensors flew.

How it addresses the challenge: MODIS and VIIRS see the same fires very differently, so a raw record jumps about 2.5× in 2012 when VIIRS arrives. After harmonization the jump falls to 1.04×. On 119 months the model never saw, it predicts VIIRS with R² 0.993, compared with 0.36 for raw MODIS. The method also holds in Ethiopia and Iraq.

Why it matters: Terra MODIS is due to stop collecting science data around January 2027, and our record carries on unbroken on NOAA-20 and NOAA-21. Using NASA FIRMS and NASA POWER, SYNTRA asks every day whether today’s fires are normal for the season, and names the areas to check. This helps agriculture, health, civil defence and humanitarian teams.
details:
What it does

SYNTRA joins NASA's two fire-watching eras into one record. MODIS has detected active fires since 2000 and VIIRS since 2012, but VIIRS sees far smaller fires, so a raw chart of Sudan's hotspots jumps 2.49 times between 2011 and 2012 although the fires did not change. We remove that seam and build one monthly fire record for Sudan from November 2000 to today, in VIIRS units, then put it to work in a story website and a Streamlit app.

How it works

1. Download: 4,462,802 hotspots from the NASA FIRMS archive (MODIS Collection 6.1, VIIRS Suomi NPP and NOAA-20) plus the near-real-time FIRMS API for 2026.

2. Clean: keep only detections inside Sudan's border, keep vegetation fires (type 0), and set aside 45,464 detections at always-hot sites such as gas flares and industry.

3. Count fairly: each 0.1° grid cell (about 11 km) counts once a day if it burned. Counting fire cell-days instead of raw pixels halves the resolution gap between the sensors.

4. Harmonize: a factor fitted for each calendar month converts MODIS into VIIRS units, because the gap is 1.4 times in November but 6.8 times in July, when wet-season fires are small. Months with only Terra (2000 to 2002) are scaled up to Terra plus Aqua first.

5. Validate: we hide one year at a time and predict it from MODIS with factors that never saw it. Over 119 held-out months, raw MODIS explains R² 0.36 of what VIIRS saw; SYNTRA explains 0.993. We ran the same test on Ethiopia (0.99) and Iraq (0.91), and we show openly that it fails in Saudi Arabia, where gas flares outnumber real fires.

6. Carry it forward: when Suomi NPP data ends, NOAA-20 times 0.986 takes over, fitted on every month both satellites flew. NOAA-21 is ready as the next handover.

What people see

- Live map: the last 24 hours and the last 7 days from five satellites, cleaned like the archive.

- Early warning: one daily call, "expected seasonal burning" or "areas to check first", comparing today with the same days in 26 fire seasons and adding NASA POWER weather.

- Status in plain words: very high, above normal, normal or below normal, with the rule that decided it shown under the card.

- Burning calendar and risk clock: every month since 2000 in one heatmap, and the fire season on a 52-week dial.

- Continuity monitor: every satellite handover with its factor, and a drift check for when MODIS stops.

Benefits and intended impact

War makes ground reports from much of Sudan hard to get, so satellites are often the only steady witness. With one consistent record, a ministry, an aid agency or a researcher can ask whether this season is worse than 2005 and get an honest answer. Farmers and agriculture planners can see when the season starts; disaster teams can see where fire is unusual today. Terra MODIS is due to stop collecting science data around January 2027, and our continuity monitor shows a fire record can stay unbroken through that change.

Tools and languages

- Python: pandas, NumPy, GeoPandas, Shapely, PyArrow, Plotly, Folium, Matplotlib, Requests, Jupyter and pytest.

- Streamlit (app, hosted on Streamlit Community Cloud).

- HTML, CSS and JavaScript with three.js for the story site, hosted on Netlify, with Netlify Functions serving the live feed and weather.

- Data: NASA FIRMS (archive and near-real-time API) and NASA POWER. Country borders from Natural Earth.

- GitHub for version control. No special hardware: everything runs on our own computers and free cloud hosting.

How it is creative

- We count burned cells per day instead of pixels, which makes two very different sensors comparable before any factor is applied.

- The 2012 seam is a 3D landscape of 300 months that flattens as you scroll, so anyone can watch the harmonization happen.

- We plan for the satellites ending: the continuity monitor builds every handover into the product from the start.

- We publish where the method fails as well as where it works.

Factors we considered

- Fairness between sensors: a separate factor for each month, because the gap changes with the season.

- False fires: gas flares and industrial heat are removed so they cannot pose as wildfires.

- Data edges: Suomi NPP starts on 20 January 2012, so January 2012 is left out of the fit; partial months are not compared with full ones.

- Honest testing: every score comes from years the model never saw.

- Access: colourblind-safe sensor colours (Okabe-Ito), a site that works on phones, and status rules written out in plain words.

- Scope: we focused on Sudan to do one country well, then checked that the method carries to other countries.
